title: We're moving from Hong Kong to Kuala Lumpur. Should we buy now or rent first?
excerpt: A Hong Kong couple with an MM2H visa and cash from selling their flat are being shown KL's priciest condos. Sean says rent for two years, think like a local, and buy for yield, not prestige.

question.asker: From W, a viewer who wrote in by email
question.context: W and her husband are moving from Hong Kong to Kuala Lumpur next year on a Malaysia My Second Home (MM2H) visa, with cash from selling their Hong Kong flat. They don't drive, want to be near the MRT and malls, and want to avoid buildings with short-stay guests; they have been shown high-end projects around Damansara Heights, TRX and KL Sentral. They also want to invest, perhaps in one unit of RM1.5 million to RM2 million in Mont Kiara or two RM1 million units near KLCC, and have been told to split units into two to raise the rent.
question.text: Should they buy now or rent first, which areas and units suit them, and is splitting a unit a good idea?

answer.quote: Don't compare with whatever projects you had back in your hometown.
answer.summary: Rent first, for about two years, keep the cash in fixed deposits or other stable investments, and explore the city like a local before buying. Prices that look cheap against Hong Kong are often the most expensive in Kuala Lumpur, and for investment buy whichever unit's rent covers its instalment, whether that is one unit or two.

reasons.title: Foreign buyers get shown the top tier
reasons.body: Agents and developers push the priciest projects to buyers converting stronger currencies. A street or two stations away, prices can halve: about RM2,000 per sq ft near TRX against RM700 to RM800 in Cheras, or about RM1,000 in Mont Kiara against RM600 to RM700 in Segambut.

reasons.title: Prices here rise slowly
reasons.body: Malaysian property has grown about 3% to 4% a year on average, with constant new launches, so renting for two years costs little in missed gains. Meanwhile they can compare Mont Kiara, Desa ParkCity, Cheras, Bangsar, Subang Jaya and Shah Alam firsthand.

reasons.title: Buy what Hong Kong can't offer
reasons.body: With a car, a gated landed home of 3,000 to 3,500 sq ft can cost about RM2 million in the Klang Valley, above the foreign-ownership minimum, and renting a landed home costs far less than a city condo with the same rent.

reasons.title: Splitting units has risks
reasons.body: Dual-key units designed by the developer are fine. Adding partitions yourself can break Kuala Lumpur's new partition rules, fail renovation approval, upset the management and leave fire insurance void.

actions: Rent in an area you like for about two years and spend weekends viewing other neighbourhoods.
Keep the sale proceeds in fixed deposits or other stable investments while you look.
For an investment unit, compare prices from developers, subsales, auctions and bulk purchase groups, and check transacted prices nearby.
Choose the unit whose rent covers its instalment, rather than buying more units that each lose money.
Check the foreign-ownership minimum price and whether short-stay letting is allowed before buying in any building.
caveat: Sean wasn't sure whether foreigners can buy non-strata landed homes, so check the state's rules first. If they are moving for a job in the city centre, paying for a prime location may be worth it.
sourceNote: Summarised from Sean's full English captions for Asking Sean #231. The quoted line is verbatim; everything else is paraphrased. Figures are as Sean stated them in November 2023; MM2H and foreign-ownership rules change, so check the current ones. Sean mentions a mortgage specialist who works for a property investment company he uses; the article leaves out her details.
